target_customer: Young women who want to swap, buy and sell fashion, first in Australia and then the US
problem: Women buy clothes they quickly tire of and rarely wear again, and wanted a way to turn unwanted items into new ones.
business_model: Consumer marketplace for fashion swapping using a virtual currency called buttons, later reworked for instant gratification on iOS
product_category: Peer to peer fashion swap and resale marketplace

founders.name: Nikki Durkin
founders.background_notes: SmartCompany says she was 18 when she founded the business and 20 when it closed. It also says she was mentored by Pollenizer co-founder Mick Liubinskas.

founders.name: Peter Delahunty
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page and named by VentureBeat at Demo Day. TechCrunch reported in September 2013 that he had left.

founders.name: Dan Walker
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder and software engineer on the YC page. TechCrunch reported in September 2013 that he had left.

exit.reason: Founder announced closing after about four years; her own account cites running out of money and technical and financial difficulties.

competitors.name: Poshmark
competitors.what: Mobile app that builds a community around selling fashion without a virtual currency, using themed online trunk shows

technical_complexity.rationale: A marketplace with a virtual currency and later an iOS app is standard engineering. The founder herself blamed technical mistakes from a failed redesign in 2011.

defensibility.rationale: A swap marketplace gains some network effect from listings, but the button currency was easy to copy and was dropped in the US, and Poshmark and others competed for the same users.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent bought or copied it directly. Resale competitors such as Poshmark and ThredUp grew while 99dresses shut down in about 2014.

market_need_then: In Australia the button swap model attracted thousands of users, and at Demo Day 2012 about 4,500 dresses had been uploaded. In the US the founder said users wanted instant gratification, which the original currency did not offer.

branding.domain_note: Used 99dresses.com. The domain now shows a Launching Soon placeholder from a GoDaddy builder with a 2025 copyright, so it is not clearly the original company.

identity.visual_style: Fashion consumer app aimed at young women
identity.voice_and_tone: Playful and hyped, as in the founder's Demo Day line that she had created crack for women

branding.brand_signature: Buttons, the virtual currency used to price and trade items (one button equaled one dollar of value)
branding.community_and_virality: TechCrunch and Fast Company coverage of the founder and Demo Day line, plus a large Australian user base, but no merch or fan accounts found.

brand_strength.rationale: The button currency and the young founder story gave it press attention, but sources show no sustained community or brand driven growth, and the US relaunch dropped the currency.

pivots.from: Web swap marketplace using a button currency
pivots.to: Mobile only iOS app with instant gratification currency
pivots.why: The button model worked in Australia but poorly in the US, and the company stopped operating in Australia.

outcome_analysis: 99dresses grew from an Australian teen's project into a YC Winter 2012 company after temporarily closing in January 2012 over cash and a botched redesign. The button currency produced engagement but not enough revenue to pay for the site and support, and the US relaunch changed the currency and went mobile only in September 2013 while two co-founders left. It never found a revenue model that beat resale rivals such as Poshmark, and the founder announced closing after about four years, around 2014.
notes: Funding conflicts. The seed round of about $105.65K dated 2012-03 rests on one database (Seedtable, seen only in a search snippet because the page returned 403); it is probably the standard YC deal but the source calls it seed. CB Insights reports about $600K across three rounds and a Pegasus Tech Ventures investment dated 2013-09, also a single database seen via snippet, with no amount. Dealroom adds Fenox Venture Capital and Tim Draper as investors, unverified and not recorded as a round. A search snippet says Durkin wrote that she signed a $1.2M seed round; that page was not opened, so the figure is unverified and no round was recorded. The Mixergy interview says only hundreds of thousands of dollars raised. Closure date: the Startup Daily and Mixergy items point to 2014 (interview dated 2014-06-27). Startup Daily and Failory were not opened in full because fetches were rate limited, so the exit reason is taken from search snippets and the SmartCompany 2012 piece, which describes the earlier temporary closure. Competitors: only Poshmark has a source dated at the batch. ThredUp, Tradesy and Threadflip appear only in undated aggregator pages and are excluded. Founder education and prior employers not found.
